title: 110: Heap Consolidation Exploit
desc: Goal: When a non-fastbin, non-tcache chunk is freed, glibc checks PREV_INUSE of the next chunk. If it's clear, the allocator consolidates backward — merging the freed chunk with the previous one. By forging a fake prev_size and clearing PREV_INUSE, you can trick consolidation into creating an overlapping chunk that spans another live allocation.
source: // Overflow b to forge c's prev_size
// consolidation: c merges backward to a
// new free chunk spans a + b + c
// big overlaps b! Write to b via big.

logs.msg: When glibc frees a chunk, it checks the PREV_INUSE bit of the next chunk's size field. If clear, the allocator reads prev_size to find the previous chunk and merges them. This is consolidation — and it trusts attacker-controllable metadata.
Allocating A (128), B (128), C (128), and a guard chunk.
free(A) — A is freed and placed in unsorted bin (no tcache in glibc 2.23; too large for fastbins). A's PREV_INUSE is cleared on B's header.

Now we simulate an overflow from B into C's header. We forge C's prev_size to point all the way back to A, and clear C's PREV_INUSE bit. This tricks free(C) into thinking A+B+C is one contiguous free region.

free(C) triggers backward consolidation. glibc reads prev_size from C → finds A (which is free) → merges A+B+C into one giant free chunk. Now malloc(384) returns a chunk that overlaps B — you have read/write access to B's data through the new allocation!

winMsg: Forging prev_size and clearing PREV_INUSE tricks backward consolidation into creating a chunk that overlaps live allocations. This is the foundation of House of Einherjar and many modern heap exploits.
